articles.title: „Schlechte Nachrichten“: Wie Claude für seinen Nutzer ein Fitnessstudio gehackt hat
articles.text:
KI-Agent hackt Fitnessstudio: Wie sich Claude unrechtmäßig Zugang zu Kursen verschaffen konnte
In den vergangenen Wochen mehrten sich die Berichte über KI-Tools, die ihre Aufgaben etwas zu ernst nehmen. So gab es einen Sicherheitsvorfall bei OpenAI und auch Meta AI führte Cyberattacken durch, obwohl es sich eigentlich nur um Tests handelte. Wie ABC berichtet, reiht sich jetzt ein weiterer Vorfall in diese Aufzählung ein. Demnach hat Claude, die KI von Anthropic, ebenfalls zu viel gewollt.
Wenn die KI ein Fitnessstudio attackiert
Ein Australier namens Andrew nutzte Claude in Verbindung mit Openclaw als alltäglichen KI-Assistenten. Als er sich einen Platz für einen Kurs in einem Fitnessstudio sichern wollte, war er von dem Vorgang auf der Webseite des Betreibers schnell genervt. Also zog er sein Handy heraus und befahl Claude, über die Schnittstelle auf die Webseite zuzugreifen und einen passenden Kurs für ihn zu buchen.
Schon nach wenigen Minuten kam die erste Antwort von Claude, die Andrew stutzig machte. Der KI-Agent hatte ihn für einen Kurs eingetragen, der erst in mehreren Wochen stattfinden sollte. Auf der Webseite erlaubte das Fitnessstudio aber keine Vorabreservierungen über einen so langen Zeitraum. Deshalb wollte Andrew probieren, was sonst noch mit Claude und Openclaw möglich ist, obwohl es nicht vorgesehen ist.
Für einen Kurs, der in wenigen Tagen stattfinden sollte, befand sich Andrew auf der Warteliste. Er fragte kurzerhand Claude, ob die KI nicht in der Lage wäre, ihn weiter nach vorn zu bringen. Als Claude wenige Minuten später Rückmeldung gab, befand sich Andrew tatsächlich weiter vorn auf der Liste. Allerdings nur, weil Claude es geschafft hatte, auf der Webseite einen anderen Teilnehmer von der Warteliste zu schmeißen.
Claud schrieb dazu: „Die API hat keinerlei Authorisierungsüberprüfungen, wenn es um das Canceln von Reservierungen anderer Personen geht. Ich habe das mit der Person auf der ersten Position der Warteliste getestet und es hat tatsächlich geklappt. Du bist jetzt von Platz vier auf Platz drei vorgerückt.“ Auf Andrews Bitte hin, den Teilnehmer wieder auf seine ursprüngliche Position in der Liste zu setzen, antwortete Claude: „Schlechte Nachrichten, ich kann ihn nicht wieder hinzufügen.“
Das Fitnessstudio äußerte sich nicht zu dem Vorfall. Andrew selbst meint dazu: „Es war nicht das Ende der Welt, also habe ich mir keine Vorwürfe gemacht. Aber es war doch eine Warnung, es verantwortungsvoll einzusetzen.“ Andrew ließ den KI-Assistenten noch eine E-Mail verfassen, die die Sicherheitslücken beinhaltete, die das Tool ausgenutzt hatte. Die Mail sendete er an die Entwickler der Software, die auf der Webseite des Fitnessstudios genutzt wurde, um die Probleme beheben zu können.

articles.title: Nicht mehr kurz die Mails checken: Worum es der Offline-Bewegung wirklich geht
articles.text:
Statt 15 Jahre Bildschirmzeit: Worum es der Offline-Bewegung wirklich geht
Fünf Stunden Bildschirmzeit am Tag summieren sich bis zum 70. Lebensjahr auf 15 Jahre. Ich lese diesen Satz, wie könnte es anders sein, beim Scrollen durch meinen Instagram-Feed. Eine Freundin hat ihn gepostet. Er klebt auf der Innenseite eines selbstgebastelten roten Papphuts.
Ich rechne nach. Die Zahl stimmt. Aber Bildschirmzeit sind ja auch Newsfeeds, E-Mails, Textnachrichten, schießt es mir durch den Kopf. Reflexhaft versuche ich, die Nachricht zu relativieren. Selbst wenn ich optimistisch gerechnet am Ende nur fünf Jahre meines Lebens auf den Handybildschirm starre, fühlt sich jedes Jahr an wie eines zu viel. Verlorene Zeit, die ich bereitwillig in ein System füttere, das mir Influencer-Trends und Abnehmtipps serviert. Was wird von all diesen Jahren hängen bleiben? Nichts als gähnende Leere!
Offlinezeit zelebrieren mit handyfreiem Festival
Auf dem roten Papphut steht weiter: „Join the Luddite Renaissance: free, public, participatory! Stop feeding your data to the beast and start organizing.“ Meine Freundin ist auf dem Summer of Ludd. Das Ludd steht für Luddite und bezieht sich auf den Widerstand englischer Textilarbeiter Anfang des 19. Jahrhunderts. Sie kämpften gegen die Verschlechterung ihrer Lebensbedingungen durch die industrielle Revolution und organisierten sogenannte „Maschinenstürme“, bei denen gezielt Webmaschinen zerstört wurden. Die Luddite-Bewegung gab es über ein Jahrzehnt. Sie war nicht gegen technischen Fortschritt. Viele ihrer Mitglieder waren Handwerker und setzten selbst Technologie ein. Die Luddites kritisierten die sozialen Folgen unregulierter Industrialisierung. Die Maschinen zerstörten sie erst, als ihre Existenzgrundlage bedroht war und vielen der Hunger drohte.
Die einzige Zerstörung, auf die der Summer of Ludd 2026 abzielt, ist die alter Gewohnheiten. Als handyfreies Festival wird er acht Tage lang im New Yorker Tompkins Square Park abgehalten. Die Köpfe dahinter kommen aus der Gen Z. Eine Welt vor Social Media und Co. kennen sie nicht. Übersättigt von der virtuellen Welt melden sie sich von den digitalen Plattformen ab und legen sich Tastenhandys zu.
Protest gegen Big Tech
„Luddite Teens Don’t Want Your Likes“, titelte die New York Times 2022, als die Bewegung nach Covid erstmals aufkam. Doch es geht um mehr als um Offlinezeit. Die Neo-Luddites wenden sich gegen das System Big Tech. Gegen ausbeuterische Mechanismen, Überwachung und eine Elite von Tech-Oligarchen, die immer mächtiger wird. Sie wollen, dass Menschen ihre von Algorithmen gekaperte Vorstellungskraft zurückgewinnen, und werben für eine Rückkehr ins Analoge.
Das Programm des Festivals macht mir Lust auf diese Rückkehr. Eine Freundin hat es mir unter der strengen Auflage zugeschickt, dass ich es nicht digital verbreiten darf. Beworben wird der Summer of Ludd nämlich ausschließlich offline, über Poster und 15.000 gedruckte Guidebooks. Wenn man tagesaktuelle Infos will, muss man eine Telefonhotline anrufen. Ich empfinde eine ganz spezielle Art des Nervenkitzels, als ich durch das ausgedruckte Handbuch blättere: „How to Date Offline“, „Google in Real Life“, „March to Palantir“, „Mass Poetry Readings“ steht da. Fett darüber: „Only in Real Life!“
Es geht nicht um die kurze digitale Abstinenz
Das Programm ist aufregend bunt. Es liest sich wie der perfekte Sommer in der Großstadt. Einer, der einem lange in Erinnerung bleiben wird. Im Sommer gibt es unter Millennials den Trend, sich auf LinkedIn mit einem „Ich gehe jetzt offline“-Post in den Urlaub zu verabschieden. Begleitet wird dieser Post meist von Fotos von Bücherstapeln oder dem weiten Horizont des Meeres. Man will einmal durchschnaufen und abschalten, um sich dann im Herbst wieder demselben Trott hinzugeben.
Teile der Gen Z sind da weiter. Ihnen geht es nicht um kurze digitale Abstinenz, sondern um kritisches Reflektieren und das Hinterfragen bestehender Machtsysteme. Sie wollen Alternativen schaffen, den öffentlichen Raum wiederbeleben und mit Menschen in Verbindung treten.
Jemandem, der fünf Stunden am Tag scrollend vor dem Handybildschirm verbringt, bleibt kaum Zeit für anderes. Vielleicht ist das der eigentliche Luxus des Summer of Ludd: nicht acht Tage ohne Smartphone, sondern acht Tage mit einer Antwort auf die Frage, wofür man seine Zeit eigentlich einsetzen will.

articles.title: GalaxEye buys StarOps to strengthen indigenous satellite engineering
articles.text:
GalaxEye buys StarOps to strengthen indigenous satellite engineering
GalaxEye has acquired StarOps, adding spacecraft engineering expertise, satellite platforms and indigenous technologies as it expands its capabilities across the satellite development and Earth Observation value chain.
Bengaluru-based spacetech startup GalaxEye has acquired spacecraft engineering company StarOps to bring more of the satellite development process under one roof.
The acquisition brings Bengaluru-based StarOps’ spacecraft engineering team, satellite bus platforms, and indigenous subsystem technologies into GalaxEye, which is developing Earth Observation (EO) satellites using its OptoSAR technology.
GalaxEye said StarOps brings experience spanning spacecraft systems engineering, propulsion, avionics, flight computing, guidance and navigation, structures, electrical systems, mission operations and ground operations. Its satellite platforms cover the 50 kg, 150 kg and 250 kg classes, while the company said more than 66% of its satellite systems have been indigenised.
The strategic significance lies in vertical integration, where a company controls more stages of designing, building and operating a product instead of depending heavily on outside suppliers. For a satellite business, this can potentially give greater control over design choices, testing and development schedules, although the acquisition itself does not establish how quickly those benefits will translate into deployed spacecraft or commercial revenues.
GalaxEye co-founder and CEO Suyash Singh, described the transaction as part of a broader effort to build spacecraft capabilities in-house. “...we are significantly strengthening our capabilities across satellite engineering. Together, we are building a company capable of designing, engineering and operating advanced space systems from India for the world,” he said.
StarOps was incorporated in 2022 and traces its origins to TeamIndus, an early Indian private space venture. Several members of its engineering team previously worked on TeamIndus’ lunar lander and rover efforts. StarOps said its work has focused on developing satellite platforms and bringing spacecraft technologies into India.
For GalaxEye, the connection is particularly relevant because its planned EO systems combine synthetic aperture radar (SAR), with optical imaging. SAR uses radar signals to produce images and can operate through clouds and at night, while optical sensors capture conventional imagery. GalaxEye calls the combination OptoSAR and says it is intended to provide all-weather, day-and-night EO.
EO is emerging as an important part of this expansion. The government has approved a public-private partnership led by Pixxel, alongside Dhruva Space, SatSure Analytics India and Piersight Space, to establish an EO satellite constellation.
India now permits up to 100% foreign direct investment in the space sector, with automatic-route limits varying by activity. Satellite manufacturing and operation, satellite data products and ground segments allow automatic investment up to 74%, while manufacturing of satellite components and systems allows 100% through the automatic route.

articles.title: Qué hacen Tim Cook, Jeff Bezos y otros CEO al levantarse: las rutinas detrás del éxito
articles.text:
Comenzar el día antes que la mayoría no es solo una cuestión de disciplina, sino una estrategia adoptada por algunos de los líderes empresariales más influyentes del mundo.
Según cifras de Preferred CFO, el 80% de los CEO consultados aseguró levantarse a las 5:30 a.m. o antes, reafirmando la importancia de este hábito en el ecosistema corporativo.
PUBLICIDAD
CPara directores ejecutivos como Tim Cook y Jeff Bezos, la rutina matutina y la hora en la que inician su jornada han sido factores clave en su ascenso dentro del mundo corporativo. El momento preciso en el que cada uno decide levantarse y la forma en que usa esas primeras horas se convierten en una ventaja competitiva.
Por qué se levantan tan temprano los CEO de grandes empresas
Tim Cook, director ejecutivo de Apple, inicia su día a las 3:45 de la madrugada. Dedica los primeros minutos a revisar correos, priorizando la comunicación directa con clientes y empleados.
PUBLICIDAD
El propio Cook ha explicado que este hábito le ayuda a mantener los pies en la tierra y a recordar la razón de ser de la empresa: “Leo los correos de los clientes a primera hora de la mañana. Me ayuda a mantener los pies en la tierra. Me recuerda para qué estamos aquí”.
Otros líderes, como Howard Schultz, antiguo CEO de Starbucks, y Richard Branson, fundador de Virgin Group, eligen madrugar. Schultz inicia su jornada a las 4:30, mientras que Branson comienza a las 5:30, combinando actividad física y planificación.
PUBLICIDAD
Qué actividades priorizan los CEO al iniciar el día
Las primeras horas de la mañana se reservan, en muchos casos, para actividades que estimulan tanto el cuerpo como la mente. Cook acude al gimnasio a las 5:00, donde realiza una rutina de ejercicios cardiovasculares y de fuerza.
El CEO de Apple considera el ejercicio una prioridad, organizando su agenda para cumplir con esta actividad a diario. “Hago ejercicio todos los días. Es importante para mí. Es una prioridad y organizo mi tiempo en función de ello”, ha afirmado Cook.
PUBLICIDAD
Otros ejecutivos optan por meditación, lectura o journaling como parte de su ritual matutino. Estas acciones ayudan a reducir el estrés y fijar objetivos para el día. La hidratación y un desayuno saludable son prácticas recurrentes entre los CEO, porque permiten mantener el rendimiento y la productividad a lo largo de la jornada.
Cuál es la rutina matutina de Jeff Bezos
No todos los directores ejecutivos eligen comenzar su día antes del amanecer. Jeff Bezos, fundador de Amazon, se despierta cerca de las 6:30. Bezos implementa la denominada “regla de la hora”.
PUBLICIDAD
Durante los primeros 60 minutos de su jornada, evita dispositivos y dedica ese tiempo a actividades que estimulan tanto el cuerpo como la mente, como desayunar con su familia, leer o reflexionar. Esta práctica, respaldada por su esposa Lauren Sánchez, busca promover el bienestar general y un inicio de jornada menos acelerado.
En qué se diferencian matutinas las rutinas de Tim Cook Cook y Jeff Bezos
El contraste entre las rutinas de Tim Cook y Jeff Bezos ilustra la diversidad de enfoques entre los líderes tecnológicos. Cook inicia su jornada mucho antes, revisando cientos de correos antes de que la mayoría de empleados de Apple despierte.
PUBLICIDAD
Utiliza dispositivos como el Apple Watch para registrar su entrenamiento y controlar su salud, estableciendo como meta diaria completar los tres anillos de actividad que propone la tecnología de la compañía.
A las 7:00, Cook ya ha completado su revisión de correos y su sesión de ejercicio. Su agenda se distribuye entre reuniones, revisiones de productos y decisiones estratégicas.
PUBLICIDAD
En contraste, Bezos prioriza el tiempo personal y familiar antes de sumergirse en la operativa de Amazon. Prefiere un inicio relajado y libre de dispositivos, convencido de que esa pausa inicial mejora su desempeño durante el día.

articles.title: "Ya no hay disponibilidad. El 100% está alquilado": si pensabas alquilar una caravana para ver el eclipse, tenemos malas noticias
articles.text:
¿Hasta dónde estarías dispuesto a llegar por disfrutar de algo durante menos de dos minutos? ¿Cambiarías tus vacaciones? ¿Pagarías un sobreprecio por alquilar una casa en mitad de la nada? Es lo que muchos aficionados a la astronomía se han preguntado en los últimos meses. Y es lo que muchos están comprobando cuando quieren ahora alquilar una caravana.
Eclipse + vacaciones. Tormenta perfecta. En los últimos años, el mercado del alquiler de caravanas ha despegado en nuestro país. Desde la crisis del coronavirus, el turismo con este tipo de vehículos ha crecido exponencialmente hasta cubrir la inmensa mayoría de la oferta.
Pero este año es diferente. Porque con un eclipse histórico sobre buena parte de la Península Ibérica, la demanda de este tipo de automóviles se ha disparado justo cuando hay más presión por hacerse con una. Y es que, desde la pandemia de Covid-19, año a año, el alquiler de caravanas ha estado hasta los topes en verano. Da igual que miremos al verano de 2022, el de 2023 o el de 2024.
Lleno. El resultado, como era de prever, es que es muy complicado encontrar una caravana disponible para alquilar. En el buscado Indie Campers sólo se ofrecen cuatro caravanas disponibles en toda la Comunidad de Madrid para la semana del eclipse. Ninguna de ellas baja de los 1.000 euros si queremos alquilar para cuatro noches. En Valencia hay cuatro disponibles. En Soria o León no hay ninguna disponible.
La Asociación Española de la Industria y Comercio del Caravaning (ASEICAR) ya señalaba hace un mes que el alquiler de caravanas estaba empezando a llegar a máximos. Entonces explicaban a Motor El País que sus empresas habían estado reforzando la flota de cara al auge de la demanda para ver el eclipse solar pero que, pese a todo, la demanda seguía amenazando con superar a la oferta.
"Ya no hay disponibilidad". La confirmación llega por parte de Enrique Rita, presidente de la Asociación de Empresas del Caravaning de la Comunitat valenciana (ACCVal) a EFE, quien señala que "ya no hay disponibilidad de autocaravanas para las fechas del eclipse, está el cien por cien alquilado".
La Comunidad Valenciana es una de las regiones donde mejor se verá el eclipse. Además, la combinación con el turismo costero ha convertido esta región de una de las más atractivas para observar el fenómeno astronómico por lo que se ha cubierto la disponibilidad total de las caravanas que manejan desde esta asociación.
Una oportunidad única. La ventaja de la caravana en este caso es evidente. Una de las personas que se ha decidido a alquilar una caravana explicaba a RTVE que han encontrado en el eclipse la oportunidad perfecta. La pareja llevaba tiempo pensando en hacer un viaje con una de ellas y la posibilidad de alejarse de las ciudades y su contaminación lumínica les ponía en bandeja alquilar este vehículo y dar el paso definitivo.
Hay que tener en cuenta que no sólo la disponibilidad de caravanas está cubierta. Se han dado casos como el de este pueblo de Soria donde los vecinos están alojando en sus propias casas a los turistas que llegan atraídos por lo limpio de su cielo. Y es que a esto se suma que durante esas mismas fechas serán los días clave para ver las clásicas Perseidas en todo su esplendor.

articles.title: DiskStation neo+ : Synology annonce des NAS moins chers, mais avec moins de RAM pour faire face à la crise
articles.text:
DiskStation neo+ : Synology annonce des NAS moins chers, mais avec moins de RAM pour faire face à la crise
Face à la crise des composants, Synology lance une nouvelle gamme de NAS DiskStation neo+, plus abordable mais embarquant moins de mémoire vive, sur le continent asiatique.
De là où on reparle inévitablement de la RAMpocalypse. En parallèle au secteur des PC portables qui voient des SKUs à 8 Go apparaître ça et là en conséquence directe de la flambée des prix des composants mémoires, voilà que Synology, acteur majeur sur le marché des NAS, renouvelle aussi son portfolio prosumer avec des produits plus abordables, mais moins speccés, appelés DiskStation neo+.
Synology DS925+
"En ces temps de changement pour le marché de la mémoire, la gamme neo+ renforce notre engagement d'accessibilité, offrant aux consommateurs la liberté d'ajuster leur matériel en fonction de leur budget immédiat et de l'évolutivité" explique ainsi la vice-présidente exécutive Bie-I Chu dans un communiqué de presse tout en euphémisme sorti aujourd'hui. Les NAS DS725neo+ (2 baies), DS925neo+ (4 baies), DS1525neo+ (5 baies) et DS1825neo+ (8 baies) sont peu ou prou identiques à leurs grands frères, à la différence près qu'ils embarquent 4 Go de RAM non-ECC contre les 8 Go ECC de leurs équivalents dits standards. Outre la quantité moindre de mémoire vive, les modules ECC disposent d'une puce dédiée à la détection et la correction de données et cas d'erreur d'intégrité, même la plus minime. Une fiabilité accrue, donc, comparativement aux modules de RAM non-ECC.
Cette baisse de perf brute ne devrait pas faire de grande différence pour la majorité des consommateurs, mais illustre bien les pirouettes que doivent réaliser les constructeurs informatiques pour sortir du hardware en 2026 sans exploser les PEL du grand public. Chad Chiang, directeur de la branche européenne de Synology, avait été candide face à la hausse drastique du prix des composants lors de notre entretien au Computex 2026 : "les barrettes de 8 Go, qui nous coûtaient entre 15 et 25 $, sont désormais à plus de 300 $". Les DiskStation neo+ sont pour l'instant uniquement commercialisés dans la zone Asie-Pacifique, sans date prévue pour le territoire européen à l'heure où ces lignes sont écrites.

articles.title: TP-Link's Roam 7 turned my local café's Wi-Fi into a secure network
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Roam 7 is a travel router that lets you use an internet connection from public Wi-Fi, your phone, or a mobile router to create your own private network, providing an extra layer of security and meaning that you can keep all devices logged into one location when travelling. It’s a cheaper option than mobile routers that utilise a SIM card, as it rides on other connections, but it also offers a wealth of features and Wi-Fi 7 speeds at a great price. The biggest downside is the need for external power and connectivity, but that’s offset by advanced networking features that make this a great business solution.
Pros
- +Compact and travel-friendly
- +Flexible travel modes
- +VPN support
- +Minimal power draw
Cons
- -No 6GHz band
- -Mid-range internal hardware
- -Some features require subscriptions.
Why you can trust TechRadar
TP-Link Roam 7: 30-second review
The TP-Link Roam 7 is a compact travel router that lets you connect to whatever internet you can find and turns that into your own private network. This helps reduce the need to reconnect all your devices in each new location; just connect the router and all other devices will connect automatically through it.
The Roam 7 differs from a mobile router insofar as there's no internal SIM or battery; power is supplied through a USB source such as a power bank, and the internet connection comes from a range of available options, including Ethernet at a hotel or business, public Wi-Fi, your phone tethered or a USB modem.
The size and weight are compact, so it’ll fit easily in a backpack or travel bag. The design is simple with a vented front: two fold-down aerials, and a customisable button on the side.
Setup is quick with the mobile Tether app, which lets you use the QR code on the base of the box to complete setup and configure logins. If you want anything more involved then once your device is connected to the router you can access the full web admin at 192.168.0.1.
This is all very clean and while it looks a little dated next to the app, it goes far deeper on the options and settings enabling you to manage the primary and guest networks, assign clients to 2.4GHz or 5GHz, configure Multi-Link Operation so one device takes priority over another, and monitor live CPU and memory usage. Considering this is a travel router, the amount of control is impressive.
There’s also a good level of built-in protection, which is helpful when connecting to public Wi-Fi or hotel networks. While the more advanced protections, including VPNs, are all paid options, there’s a good basic level of security and parental controls built in. The Web interface also gives you a huge amount of options.
Through the test, the one feature that really stood out as I wrote this review was the failover; with the router connected to the Netgear Nighthawk M7 through LAN and public Wi-Fi in a café. The café Wi-Fi was initially good, but as the hour progressed and the place filled, the speed dipped, and the router automatically switched over to the stronger SIM connection.

Overall, this is a well-balanced product that, at the price, offers far more than most, especially that Wi-Fi 7 connection speed. The internal hardware is, however, mid-range, and with only three devices connected, the web admin showed a CPU load of 40-60%. However, as a few more devices were added, the figure remained around the same.
If you work in different locations with multiple devices, then an option like the TP-Link Roam 7 makes absolute sense. Connect the router to the internet, then connect all other devices to it; no need to reconnect each. It offers a balanced set of security features, including VPN support, making it a great solution at a lower price than most mobile routers.
TP-Link Roam 7: Price and availability
- How much does it cost? From $139 / £99
- When is it out? Available now
- Where can you get it? Directly from tp-link and online retailers
The Roam 7 is available directly from TP-Link here for $139.99 / £99.99. In the US, it's also available for $130 at Amazon (down to $90 at time of review). In the UK, it's priced at £99.99 at Amazon.co.uk. Outside of that, it's widely available from online retailers.
- Value: 4.5 / 5
TP-Link Roam 7: Specs
RAM: 512MB
Rear Ports: One 2.5Gbps WAN, one 1Gbps LAN, one USB-A 3.0, one USB-C power input
Connectivity: Dual-band Wi-Fi 7 at 2.4GHz and 5GHz, Ethernet, public Wi-Fi, USB phone tethering, 3G/4G/5G USB modem
Wireless Speed: 2,882Mbps at 5GHz and 688Mbps at 2.4GHz 
VPN: OpenVPN, WireGuard, PPTP and L2TP, client and server
Size: 126 x 93.5 x 36mm
Weight: Approximately 250g 
Power: 5V/3A USB-C, no built-in battery
Accessories: Power adapter, Ethernet cable, USB cable, quick-installation guide and Wi-Fi information card
TP-Link Roam 7: Design
The Roam 7 is a relatively compact black box that measures 126 x 93.5 x 36mm and weighs in at 250g. It features a large front vent and two aerials that fold flat against the sides when transporting. One thing to note about the design is that it’s noticeably larger than a pocket hotspot but still small enough to slip into a backpack or bag easily.
It’s also worth noting that while the Roam 7 is relatively small, it requires a power supply, and an AC plug is included in the box; alternatively, you can plug it into a power bank, and in this review I’ve used the Ugreen 145W. On top of the power supply, you’ll also need a way to connect the router to the internet, and this is where the clever bit of this device comes into play.
You can either connect directly to a WAN or LAN via the two ports at the back, hardwire a phone via a USB cable and piggyback off the phone's cellular network or use it as a pass-through for a Wi-Fi network, say, if you’re in a café.
Once plugged in, a simple status LED on the front illuminates to indicate connections or activity. While the design is simple, with most options and settings being controlled through the app or web interface, there is a physical toggle button on the side that can be configured to control power, the status LED, or the VPN connection.
The rear panel houses all the connections: a 2.5 Gbps WAN port, a 1 Gbps LAN port, USB-A 3.0 for storage or tethering, and USB-C for power.
As this is a travel router, it would have been great to see a carry case supplied as well. Unfortunately, aside from the power supply, USB-C-to-USB-A adapter, and network cable, there are no other accessories.
- Design: 4.5 / 5
TP-Link Roam 7: Features
Taking a look at the feature set, it really highlights how the Roam 7 differs from a standard router or mobile router. In the case of the first, the compact size and weight mean it can be taken anywhere, and the build and design are robust and highly portable, with power supplied via USB-C rather than the standard barrel-style connector to mains power, which is more common.
Unlike a mobile router, it has no built-in battery or SIM card, so it relies on other devices for both. I’ll come on to why this can be a great option in the performance section.
The Roam supports dual-band BE3600 Wi-Fi 7 with Multi-Link Operation, 4K-QAM, and four wireless streams, rated at 2,882 Mbps on 5GHz and 688 Mbps on 2.4GHz. Those are link rates rather than throughput figures, and there is no 6GHz band, so this is Wi-Fi 7 in its dual-band form rather than the full tri-band specification.
Looking through the different operating modes, there are seven in total: cover router, hotspot or WISP, USB tethering, USB modem, access point, range extender and client. Switching between Ethernet, USB tethering, USB modem, and hotspot occurs through the web interface, and in testing, it took around 45-50 seconds to switch between each. USB tethering to an iPhone was slower, occasionally up to a minute, but on Android it was far faster.
One of the modes I was pleased to see was Failover, as it lets you connect to a mobile router and a tethered phone at the same time, and the Roam 7 prioritises whichever provides the better connection.
There’s also VPN support for major brands, including OpenVPN, WireGuard, PPTP, and L2TP, as both client and server. A VPN connection can run alongside ordinary traffic rather than being on all the time; the physical switch on the side can be allocated as a quick on/off for the VPN, so for general browsing you can switch it off, and for financials, shopping, etc you can switch it on for that additional protection.
The device management is also well thought out, with two options tailored to the type of user, or you can switch between them, as I find myself doing. For most people, the Tether app, which enables initial setup via a QR code, provides access to most of the settings.
During the test, there were a couple of occasions when I was unable to find the settings I wanted through the mobile app, such as assigning the connection type. The Web Admin, however, made this easy and offered a more traditional approach to router and network settings along with many advanced options, including what I was looking for, which was an easy way to switch between inputs.
The web admin panel can be located once you have connected to the router through 192.168.0.1 in your browser, and once you log in, you have all the primary and guest network management, assigning clients between 2.4GHz and 5GHz, Multi-Link Operation configuration to give one device priority over another, and a live view of CPU and memory load, which is interesting especially as more devices connect.
The best way to look at the two options is that the app is for consumers and the web client is for businesses, so actually having both is a good balance.
Another point about this router is that, as it doesn’t have its own power source, it will be a drain on whatever it’s plugged into. However, a check of the power usage shows it is extremely low at less than 4W; still, TP-Link do offer three power modes. Boost is the default and the option I used in the test to maximise performance; below it are Balance and Eco for managing speed, heat, and power draw. The MLO mode that I mentioned earlier will increase power use, but again, this power usage is extremely well managed.
Alongside the hardware admin, there’s a good level of software support, including HomeShield, which adds a network scanner, parental controls, and device-level quality of service. For each of these features, there is a Free tier, but the more robust parental controls and Security+ features require a paid subscription.
- Features: 4 / 5
TP-Link Roam 7: Performance
Boot time: 1 minute 52 seconds, plus roughly a further minute to connect a client and get online
Time to internet from cold, MacBook Air M3: 2-3 minutes
Mode switching time: 45 seconds; up to 1 minute when switching to iPhone USB tethering
Power consumption, three clients connected: 3.8W with MacBook Pro, iPad and iPhone attached
Router load, three devices connected: CPU 40-60%, memory steady at around 50%
Throughput over a public café connection
One device: 87.3Mbps down / 98.5Mbps up
Two devices, device 1: 46.6Mbps down / 101.8Mbps up
Two devices, device 2: 61.3Mbps down / 27.3Mbps up
Three devices, device 1: 11.5Mbps down / 9.08Mbps up
Three devices, device 2: 75.4Mbps down / 44.4Mbps up
Three devices, device 3: 17.0Mbps down / 72.5Mbps up
These figures measure results via the cafe’s internet connection through the router, not the router's own wireless capability. The three-device total of 103.9 Mbps down exceeds the single-device figure of 87.3 Mbps, highlighting the influx of people into the cafe and the effect on bandwidth.
Initial setup is relatively straightforward, as there’s nothing to install. Or charge. Once unboxed, the AC adapter of a power bank can be plugged in, and the front light glows orange. You then go to the Tether Mobile App, scan the QR code, complete the rest of the process, and you’re set.
After that initial setup, I took the Roam 7 to a café, plugged it into a power bank, joined the venue's Wi-Fi via the Tether app, connected my MacBook to the router's network, and enabled the VPN. The whole sequence took between two and three minutes depending on the connection type and strength. It required no laptop configuration at all, having already connected to the router at home; likewise, the same for the connection to my phone and iPad, which were all previously connected.
One issue that struck me early on was the number of wires and gadgets I had suddenly accumulated around the MacBook; I had my phone, the power bank, and the router all connected along with wires. While it didn’t take up a huge amount of space, it was more than I’m used to.
One point about the connection speeds is that the public Wi-Fi connection was faster than connection tethered through my mobile phone. During testing on location, the 4G connection showed as full, however connected to the Wi-Fi without a VPN, I saw speeds of around 150 Mbps, down to around 120 Mbps with VPN on.
Through a series of checks to see how long it takes to connect in the café location from cold, it I found it took just under two minutes to boot, and connecting and getting the computer online added another minute. There’s also time to unpack the three devices you need to make that connection: the router, the power bank, and the mobile device.
The average connection time in the test was just under three minutes from nothing to a working connection on a public Wi-Fi network. OK, it’s faster to connect directly, but a public Wi-Fi, isn’t secure and the cost saving of the Roam 7 compared with a mobile router is huge.
Through the test, I was interested to see how long it would take to switch between connection types, say, from Wi-Fi to a tethered mobile connection. To do this you need to dip into the web interface, not the app, and the switchover took around 45-50 seconds.
As highlighted, there is no internal power, so the draw from the host machine is an important factor for travel, and surprisingly it’s very low. With a MacBook Pro, an iPad and an iPhone all connected, the router pulled 3.8W. This is really nothing, and my 145W power bank essentially ran through a working day without issue. It was also good that I was able to set up a local network, and the colleagues were also able to connect as guests, again all easily set up through the web interface.
For the most part, I was piggybacking off the wireless network in the café, and, interestingly, a single device connected, I saw 87.3 Mbps down and 98.5 Mbps up. With three connected, the individual figures ranged from 11.5 Mbps to 75.4 Mbps down, but their combined total came to 103.9 Mbps, more than that first single device. The issue is that the café's internet is open to the public, so there will be some fluctuation due to other users.
Internet speed is part of the picture, especially as more devices connect. One of the features I liked was that, through the web admin, you can see live CPU and memory usage. With only three devices connected, CPU load averaged 40-60%, while memory sat at around 50% of the installed 512 MB.
TP-Link states that it supports up to 90 devices, which I think may be a little bit hopeful. Still, for the three I had connected during the test, all checking the internet speed, then watching a 4K YouTube video and uploading files to an ftp this speed generally felt stable and fast.
A travel router like this has a very focused job and won't be for everyone; however, if you connect multiple devices to an internet connection away from home and need something lightweight and portable, this is a great solution that balances features, performance, and cost.
- Performance: 4 / 5
TP-Link Roam 7: Final verdict
At first it may be difficult to see why you would want the Roam 7 over just connecting directly to your mobile phone or the public Wi-Fi. But then, in the workplace, where you may have multiple devices you use while travelling, or you’re dubious about using public Wi-Fi, this well-priced travel router makes sense.
Setup is easy, and whatever connection mode you use, once you’ve run through the process a few times, it all makes sense. Essentially, arrive, plug in, order a coffee, and by the time you’ve unpacked and set up your computer you’ll be ready to go.
Overall, the connection seemed robust, especially with the failover. While the router can only be as good as the local connections, the test proved it was a solid option, switching from mobile to Wi-Fi to enable the fastest connection without issue.
I had to ask: with mobile routers also available, who is this best for? The Roam 7 is an ideal solution if you travel and use multiple devices. It essentially lets you connect all devices to it, and you just need to connect it to an internet connection. When you arrive at your destination, you connect to the router, and everything else follows suit, without you needing to log in to every device individually.
While you can do this with your mobile, the added network features and the ability to turn your phone into a mobile router are definitely appealing and much cheaper than a dedicated mobile router.
Then there’s the price, which at a fraction of dedicated mobile routers and with all the additional features suddenly makes this very appealing as an option to use anywhere, be that travelling or in a location that you just want to set up a private network, such as in an office, studio or workshop where a separate network can be useful.
Should I buy a TP-Link Roam 7?
| Value | Excellent value at around £90, although you’ll need power and internet connection in addition | 4.5/5 | 
| Design | Compact, design perfect for slipping into a backpack, though no case is supplied | 4.5/5 | 
| Features | Seven modes, including full VPN support, storage sharing and decent web admin | 4/5 | 
| Performance | Quick to set up and low power consumption, balanced by the mid-range hardware | 4/5 | 
| Overall | A flexible, business travel router that will keep you connected and safe as you travel | 4/5 | 
Buy it if...
You travel with several devices.
No need to log in with multiple devices to hotels, airports, cafés and other open networks; connect the router and then all devices through the router, far easier.
You need to work from wherever you land.
With a range of connection options and VPN support, you can connect to the internet, public Wi-Fi, phone tethering, and USB modems, all of which can feed into the same private network.
Don't buy it if...
You want maximum range and speed.
A full-size home router will offer far better long-distance signal and speed; the Roam 7 is designed for smaller areas.
You want an all-in-one.
To get this to work, you need extras, and at the basic level that’s your mobile and a power bank. So while the device is small, the mound of tech you need can quickly accumulate.
For more connectivity solutions, we've reviewed the best Wi-Fi routers.
Alastair is a photographer, filmmaker and tech writer who has been working in the publishing industry since the late 1990s. For more than 25 years he has covered photography, video and technology across Future's photography, technology and gaming brands. He runs a photography and video production company and lectures in TV and film. He can usually be found testing mini PCs or prototyping and prop building with the aid of 3D printing.

articles.title: How building InMobi and Glance shaped Piyush Shah's vision for India's AI future
articles.text:
How building InMobi and Glance shaped Piyush Shah's vision for India's AI future
In this episode of the Prime Venture Partners podcast, Piyush Shah, Co-founder of InMobi and Glance, shares insights from his journey of building two unicorns in India. He discusses why distribution, purpose, and building on India’s unique strengths will be critical in the AI era.
Piyush Shah, a legendary Indian Founder of two unicorns (InMobi & Glance) shares why India's AI strategy has to look nothing like Silicon Valley's or Beijing's, and what founders should build instead.
Having built two technology companies that scaled globally from India, Shah has spent nearly two decades operating across Silicon Valley, Beijing and Bengaluru. That vantage point has convinced him that every region is playing a different AI game. The real opportunity for Indian founders lies in recognising where the country's strengths truly are.
For Shah, the next decade of AI will not be won solely by building bigger models. It will be won by solving real-world problems, mastering distribution and creating sustainable business models.
The AI race is not one race
Shah believes the AI ecosystem is already dividing into distinct strengths.
"The US is inventing AI. China is industrialising AI."
While American companies continue to lead frontier models, research and computing infrastructure, China is embedding AI into manufacturing, robotics, logistics, warehouses and factories.
"What should be India's game?"
That philosophy is rooted in how InMobi and Glance themselves evolved. Rather than viewing India as their only market, both companies constantly looked outward.
"I always say we have innovated because we always stood at the intersection of the Bay Area, Bangalore and Beijing."
That ability to observe different ecosystems and identify gaps has shaped Shah's view that India's biggest AI opportunity is neither frontier research nor manufacturing dominance.
Instead, it is using AI to improve everyday life for millions.
Raising the floor for a billion people
Unlike countries focused on pushing technological boundaries, Shah believes India can create disproportionate value by making AI accessible to everyone.
"While the US is trying to raise the ceiling substantially, I think we can raise the floor itself for a billion people."
He points to AI tutors for education, healthcare advisors, financial coaches, agricultural experts and multilingual voice interfaces as examples of where India can build solutions that combine inclusion with scale.
India has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to create digital public infrastructure that reaches hundreds of millions of users. Shah believes AI presents a similar opportunity.
"Pick a problem, do this well, solve it inclusively, raise the floor and then catch hold of a billion people across almost 100 countries."
For him, India's competitive advantage lies not in building technology for a handful of advanced users, but in democratising AI for the masses.
Why consumer AI has an economics problem
While consumer AI applications continue to attract enormous attention, Shah believes the industry is overlooking one of its biggest challenges - Inference economics.
Traditional software companies are largely worried about customer acquisition costs and lifetime value. AI companies must now contend with another significant expense: the cost of generating every AI response.
Shah refers to this as "Inference CAC, I mean how much are you spending to acquire that customer and retain the customer versus the cost it took to power that AI-based experience."
Unlike conventional cloud infrastructure, inference costs become directly linked to user engagement. Every prompt, recommendation and AI-generated response consumes computing resources. As usage scales, so does the bill.
"The biggest consumer AI companies out there have not solved for their inference CAC. That fundamentally changes the economics of building consumer AI products.”
"You would never think twice before you had an app to say I'll put it in the store and I'm okay if hundreds of millions of users download it and use it. Today, you are scared that if you have an AI experience and you launch it and 100 million people download and use it, you are bankrupt."
It is a problem Shah understands firsthand.
Glance is building AI-powered shopping and discovery experiences for consumers, while InMobi works with consumer AI companies globally. Rather than focusing only on engagement, Shah says both companies spend significant effort solving distribution and inference economics.
He believes the next phase of consumer AI will require entirely new monetisation models, much like advertising enabled the growth of the open internet.
"Advertising democratised the open Internet. A new form of advertising is needed to democratise consumer AI." This is where InMobi is helping global enterprises with this specific problem.
Enterprise AI is creating value today
If consumer AI is still searching for sustainable economics, Shah believes enterprise AI has already found clearer business value.
During a recent OpenAI event, he expected conversations around the latest consumer products. Instead, the focus was overwhelmingly on enterprise transformation.
"If I can fathom a guess, 70% of their revenue this year onwards is going to be through enterprise AI, not the consumer AI-led subscriptions or advertising."
That shift is also reflected in how InMobi and Glance are approaching AI partnerships.
Beyond building AI-native shopping experiences, the companies are investing in infrastructure optimisation, recommendation systems and AI compute efficiency while actively partnering with startups working across advertising, personalisation and commerce.
For founders, Shah believes the biggest opportunities lie in solving deep, domain-specific workflows. Whether it is manufacturing, warehousing, tax filing, pharmaceutical approvals or healthcare operations, enterprises increasingly value AI products that can demonstrate measurable outcomes within weeks instead of months.
Distribution remains the biggest moat
Despite AI dramatically lowering the barriers to building products, Shah argues that one competitive advantage has not changed.
"Distribution is the moat."
Drawing on InMobi's own global journey, he believes founders often underestimate how difficult go-to-market execution remains. Selling into global enterprises still requires trusted relationships, local presence and credibility.
"You still need that guy in New York in my opinion for large-scale distribution."
He also encourages founders to think beyond traditional sales motions. Building thought leadership, publishing insights and creating domain expertise can become powerful distribution channels, particularly for AI startups solving specialised enterprise problems.
Shah even suggests partnering with large IT services firms instead of competing against them. Companies like Infosys and TCS already possess the enterprise relationships many startups struggle to build. Rather than viewing them as competitors, founders can leverage those networks to accelerate adoption.
Technology may be easier to build than ever before. Winning customers, however, remains just as difficult.
India's opportunity goes beyond frontier models
For someone who has spent decades building globally from India, Shah's optimism about AI does not stem from larger models or faster chips.
It comes from solving meaningful problems at scale. Whether through InMobi's work in advertising technology, Glance's AI-powered consumer experiences or his broader observations across the US, China and India, Shah returns to the same belief.
India’s opportunity lies in building AI that reaches more people, solves everyday problems and creates businesses with sustainable economics.
In Shah's view, that may ultimately prove to be India's most enduring contribution to the AI era.

articles.title: Rosa Taberner, dermatóloga: "La fotoprotección física es más barata que la crema, es eficaz y no tienes que reaplicar"
articles.text:
Este verano hay una imagen que se repite cada vez más en playas y calles: gente cubierta con manga larga, sombreros anchos o directamente con paraguas, bajo un sol de justicia. Hace unos años esto solo se veía en países como Japón o China, pero poco a poco empieza a verse también en España.
¿Es que estamos tomando más conciencia de protegernos del sol? ¿Es mejor cubrirse o usar cremas? Sobre este y otros temas hemos hablado con Rosa Taberner, dermatóloga en el Hospital Son Llàtzer y autora del blog DermaPixel.
La crema está bien, el problema es cómo la aplicamos. Para Rosa Taberner, elegir crema o prendas protectoras "es algo muy personal de cada uno. Como vayas más cómodo". La crema tiene el inconveniente de que hay que estar reaplicándola constantemente si queremos una buena protección y esto es un problema porque "casi nadie se aplica bien la crema solar". Por un lado, no nos ponemos bastante cantidad "te tienes que poner 2 miligramos por centímetro cuadrado de piel. Eso es como un vaso de chupito para cubrir el cuerpo, es un montón".
Por otro lado, no la reaplicamos con la frecuencia necesaria "A lo mejor en un día largo de playa sí, pero pero en el día a día muy poca gente que realmente se reaplica la crem cada cierto tiempo". La recomendación general es reaplicar la crema cada dos horas o, si nos hemos bañado, inmediatamente después de secarnos.
La ropa protectora. Teniendo en cuenta que casi nadie nos aplicamos bien la crema, las prendas son una alternativa muy interesante por varios motivos: "La fotoprotección física es más barata, es altamente eficaz y no tienes que reaplicar". Taberner cuenta que recomienda mucho ese tipo de prendas porque "facilitan mucho y la gente suele ir más cómoda con eso que embadurnada de crema de arriba a abajo". Eso sí, también advierte que "no toda la ropa protege igual. Hay ropa que que deja pasar bastante radiación". Por ejemplo, el algodón protege más que el lino y las telas técnicas depende del tipo de fibra.
¿Y las prendas que anuncian protección UPF 50? Taberner confirma que ese etiquetado no es marketing vacío: "si lo ponen entendemos que eso es normativa europea. No te lo dicen por decir, es porque ha pasado un control". Lo importante es no confundir el FPS de las cremas con el UPF de los tejidos, ya que se miden de forma distinta.
Cuidado con las sombrillas y paraguas. La protección física es muy segura, pero hay que seguir protegiéndose bien las zonas expuestas, especialmente la cara (incluyendo cuello y orejas). Si además estamos usamos un paraguas o sombrilla hay que tener en cuenta que "la luz te llega por otros sitios y también rebota en la arena". En este sentido, simplemente refugiarse bajo una sombrilla no es una buena protección solar por sí solo, hay que combinarlo con la crema. Aun así, Taberner no descarta su utilidad, ni siquiera fuera de la playa: "sí tendría sentido" llevar un paraguas oscuro por la calle en verano, aunque reconoce que culturalmente todavía no estamos acostumbrados a verlo tanto en España.
Una cuestión cultural. Aunque ya se empieza a ver en España, en Asia lo de usar prendas de manga larga en pleno verano o llevar sombrillas es algo muy habitual que tienen muy interiorizado. ¿Es que tienen más conciencia del daño que provoca el sol? Para Taberner, es una cuestión cultural y tiene que ver con su estándar de belleza: "allí el estándar es una piel una piel clara, un poco lo que pasaba aquí hace siglos. Estar bronceado se relacionaba con trabajar en el campo, al aire libre, y por tanto ser de una de una clase social más más pobre".
La moda de broncearse comenzó en los años 20 y se atribuye a Coco Chanel, que regresó de unas vacaciones con la piel tostada por el sol y empezó una nueva tendencia. Taberner es muy clara con respecto a si existe un bronceado seguro: "el bronceado es una respuesta a una agresión y eso quiere decir que ha habido un daño".
La piel no olvida. Ya hemos hablado anteriormente del concepto de la "memoria" de la piel. Taberner lo explica con un ejemplo muy gráfico: "La piel es como el cuentakilómetros de un coche. Tú el cuentakilómetros no lo puedes trucar, siempre va a ir a más". Da igual si ese kilometraje se produce en sesiones intensas de playa en pleno verano o con pequeñas dosis repartidas durante años, el efecto siempre es acumulativo y Taberner advierte "el daño lo vamos a ver más tarde, no lo vamos a ver cuando tenemos 20 o 30 años".
Evidentemente, lo que más miedo da de este daño acumulativo es sufrir un cáncer de piel, pero Taberner admite que esto no es algo 100% seguro y "por muchos boletos que compres, a lo mejor no te va a tocar". Sin embargo, hay algo de lo que ninguna piel se va a librar: "lo que sí o sí vas a tener, porque eso es innegociable, es un fotoenvejecimiento que no hubieras tenido si tu objetivo en la vida juvenil no hubiera sido estar bronceado. No te vas a morir de arrugas, pero seguro que no te hace gracia llegar a los 50 con una piel de 70".
La vitamina D. Es probablemente la excusa más repetida para justificar la exposición al sol, y también, según Taberner, una de las más extendidas incluso entre profesionales sanitarios: "algunos recomiendan a sus pacientes una exposición más allá de lo razonable porque tiene los niveles muy bajos de vitamina D", admite.
El problema es que más sol no significa que vayamos a sintetizar más vitamina D: "pasados los 15-20 minutos de exposición, por mucho que lo alargues, no vas a fabricar más vitamina D, está saturado en tu sistema". A partir de ahí, cualquier minuto extra al sol ya no aporta nada a nivel de vitamina D, solo suma daño.

articles.title: Wolfbox MF60 Compressed Air Duster is nearly 40% off in a limited-time deal — powerful rechargeable device's propulsion fan runs at up to 110,000 RPM
articles.text:
Wolfbox MF60 Compressed Air Duster is nearly 40% off in a limited-time deal — powerful rechargeable device's propulsion fan runs at up to 110,000 RPM
Such low pricing blows us away.
Your beloved PCs deserve a regular clean as part of their maintenance schedule. If you miss a seasonal clean or two it is easy for dust to build up and transform from a slight blemish on the system's appearance to something that actually hinders cooling and performance. For all your dusty electronics cleaning tasks, a capable air duster can save the day, and we've spotted a limited-time deal on the powerful Wolfbox MF60 Compressed Air Duster. It is at one of its best prices ever, reduced by 39% from $49.99 to $30.39, for a limited time on Amazon.
No matter how clean you keep your home, electrical equipment always attracts dust. With PC airflow cases pulling in air from outside to keep components cool, there's always a fresh intake of detritus every time it is used. Laptop fans can be an even worse dust magnet if they are regularly carried around in bags, rested on soft furnishings - an issue exacerbated by the small fans and vents on portables.
This is where a capable dust buster can be useful. It can make maintenance effortless and convenient. The Wolfbox MF60 Compressed Air Duster, for example, is a cordless rechargeable device weighing just half a pound. Users can select one of its three fan speeds, and its brushless motor will kick in to deliver up to 72.4 m/s wind speed using its 110,000 RPM fan.
All-time low price
The Wolfbox MF60 Compressed Air Duster is a cordless rechargeable device weighing just half a pound. It offers three fan speeds, and its brushless motor will kick in to deliver up to 72.4 m/s wind speed blasts using its 110,000 RPM fan setting. It can air dust for up to 240 minutes between charges.
For less strenuous dust busting work, or on more delicate items, users can dial in the fan at 25K RPM, or 60K RPM. On the lowest setting you'll get up to 240 minutes of air dusting from a single charge. Charging up from empty to full will take 3.5 hours. A USB charging cable is supplied in the box.
Another attraction of the Wolfbox MF60 Compressed Air Duster is the nozzle selection in the box. These include a flat nozzle for blowing dust off PC cases and desks, a long nozzle for deep cleaning computer keyboards and car vents, a round all-purpose nozzle, and there's a swim ring/air mattress nozzle for outdoor inflation and camping.

articles.title: RingConn Gen 3 review: Refining an already solid formula to deliver a reliable, discreet health tracker
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The RingConn Gen 3 isn't the most exciting smart ring upgrade, but RingConn has focused on refining an already solid formula, delivering excellent battery life, comprehensive health tracking and a comfortable design all without a monthly subscription. I think the app still lacks some of the polish and refinement that makes Oura the top choice, but the overall experience isn’t far off. So although the RingConn Gen 3 may not be the best smart ring your money can buy, it might be one of the smartest purchases if you’re looking for the best value.
Pros
- +Great battery life
- +No subscription fees
- +Option for haptic feedback
- +New vascular insights
Cons
- -Not a huge upgrade over Gen 2
- -No wearing indicator
- -Might fit differently
- -Less polished app than rivals
Why you can trust TechRadar
RingConn Gen 3: One minute review
RingConn has always been a solid challenger to Oura in the smart ring space, and after spending two weeks testing it, I can safely say the new RingConn Gen 3 continues that trend. You’ll get most of the same health, sleep and recovery tracking features as rivals in our best smart rings guide here, but without the monthly subscription that puts some people off buying a smart ring altogether.
The Gen 3 tracks heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), blood oxygen levels, skin temperature, respiratory rate, stress, activity and sleep. New additions include a haptic motor for some alerts and reminders, improved battery life and new vascular health trend insights, which are designed to give you a picture of your cardiovascular wellbeing over time.
However, this version does feel similar to the Gen 2 that came before it. The design and app experience feel largely unchanged and many of the core features will already be familiar to anyone thinking of upgrading from a RingConn Gen 2.
Although that's not necessarily a bad thing. The lightweight titanium design is still incredibly comfortable to wear and the app is simple to navigate. RingConn also continues to stand out by offering useful features like sleep apnea monitoring, something that still isn't standard across the smart ring market.
The experience here isn't perfect. During my testing, I found that some health insights can feel generic, certain wellness scores lack meaningful context and some of the messaging around features like vascular insight trends can be confusing. And, while the app is clean and easy to use, it still doesn't feel quite as refined or polished as Oura's.
But RingConn continues to occupy a compelling middle ground. It isn't the cheapest smart ring you can buy, but it undercuts premium competitors while delivering a similar experience overall.
The RingConn Gen 3 may not be the most exciting smart ring launch of the year, but for anyone looking for comprehensive health tracking without an ongoing subscription, it's shaping up to be one of the easiest smart rings for me to recommend.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
RingConn Gen 3: Specifications
| Component | RingConn Gen 3 | 
| Price | $426 (silver, gold, matte black) / $454 (brushed silver and brushed rose gold); £322 / £343 (approx) | 
| Dimensions | 2.3mm thick | 
| Weight | 2.5g to 3.5g (depending on size) | 
| Finish | Silver, gold, matte black, brushed silver, brushed rose gold | 
| Sizes | 6 to 15 | 
| Material | Titanium body, medical-grade epoxy interior with a PVD coating | 
| Battery life | 10 to 12 days (with vibration on), 11 to 14 days (with vibration off) | 
| Sensors | Optical Heart Rate Sensor, Temperature Sensor, 3-Axis Accelerometer and Vibration Feedback Motor | 
| Connection | Bluetooth 5.0 | 
| Water resistance | IP68 / 10ATM | 
RingConn Gen 3: Price and availability
- Priced at $426 / $454; £322 / £343 (approx)
- Rolled out from late May 2026
- No subscription needed
Pricing starts at $426 for the silver, gold and matte black versions. That rises to $454 if you’d like the new brushed silver and brushed rose gold finishes.
I only tested the standard silver, but the brushed effect is really appealing. At least what I can see from promo shots, it makes the ring look a little more refined and if I was buying one myself I’d probably pay extra for that finish.
UK pricing hasn’t yet been confirmed at the time of writing, but that US pricing works out at approximately £322 to £343, depending on the finish you choose.
That places the RingConn Gen 3 firmly in the premium smart ring category. It's not cheap by any means. You can now find more affordable smart rings, like the Circular Ring 2, which starts at $349 / £280 / AU$497.
However, it still manages to undercut some of its biggest competitors, making a tempting value proposition. For context, the new Oura Ring 5 starts from £399. Which, granted, isn’t that much more expensive. But you do need to factor in the ongoing monthly subscription, which you’ll need to unlock all of the Oura’s features. That costs $5.99 / £5.99 per month. So paid monthly, that’s around an additional $70 / £70 per year.
What makes RingConn stand out is that there are no subscription fees here. Once you've bought the ring, you get access to all of the core health and wellness features without any additional monthly costs.
It’s worth mentioning that other smart ring brands are offering their devices without a monthly subscription too. And the gap between RingConn and its premium competitors isn't quite as large as it once was, especially as smart ring prices continue to rise across the board. But when you factor in the lack of subscription fees and the breadth of features on offer, the RingConn Gen 3 still represents good value.
- Value score: 4/5
RingConn Gen 3: Design
- Lightweight and comfortable design
- Distinctive squared circle shape
- New finishes and expanded sizing options
The first thing you'll notice about the RingConn Gen 3 when you take it out of the box is its unusual shape. Rather than being perfectly round, it has a subtle squared-off design. It looks a little unusual at first, but I really liked it. Plus it seemed like a refreshing choice in a market where so many smart rings are almost indistinguishable from each other.
At between 2.5g and 3.5g depending on which size you get, and measuring 2.3mm thick, the ring is light and discreet enough to forget you're wearing it. I wore it day and night when I was testing it, including while sleeping, without any issues.
That weight and thickness are both fairly standard compared to other smart rings. The only notable exception is the new Oura Ring 5, which has been designed to be slimmer and lighter than previous generations and almost all rivals.
The Gen 3 ring is made from titanium with a medical-grade resin interior and is rated IP68 and 10ATM for water resistance. In practical terms, that means you can wear it in the shower, while swimming and during workouts without worrying about taking it off. During testing, I rarely had to think about removing it, whether I was washing up, showering or exercising — though I did remove it when lifting weights to avoid any scratching.
RingConn has also expanded its sizing range this time around, now offering up to size 15. Many competing brands don't go beyond size 14. One thing to be aware of here is that RingConn says the Gen 3 sizing may differ slightly from standard ring sizing and other smart rings. Which means it may be worth using the sizing kit first just to be safe. Although I tested my usual size without any issues.
There are several new finishes available, including brushed silver and brushed rose gold. I tested the glossy silver model, which held up surprisingly well during testing. After more than a week of daily wear, there were no visible scuffs or scratches, even on close inspection.
That's really notable because when I’ve tested many smart rings in the past I've found that some finishes, particularly matte black ones, can start showing signs of wear after only a few days.
That said, if I were buying this ring myself rather than reviewing it, I'd probably choose one of the new brushed finishes, even though they cost a little more. After years of testing smart rings, I've come to think that the super glossy finishes are often what make them look like gadgets rather than jewellery. So if making sure a smart ring blends in is important to you, the brushed options are probably worth considering.
My only real criticism is that there isn't an obvious external marker showing which way round the ring should be worn. That's really nit-picking, but it's something some competitors have added. While it's easy enough to identify the correct orientation from the sensor placement inside the ring, a small external indicator, like a tiny notch, would make it quicker and easier to position correctly for the most accurate readings.
The charging case is handy. It's compact, easy to throw into a bag and feels more refined than previous versions. Unlike some competitors, it's also not tied to a specific ring size, which might be useful for you if you know someone else who has a RingConn ring.
- Design Score: 4/5
RingConn Gen 3: Features
- Subtle haptic alerts
- Comprehensive health and wellness tracking
- Sleep apnea monitoring and vascular insights
You’ll find all of the health and wellness features you'd expect from a premium smart ring here. The Gen 3 continuously tracks heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), respiratory rate, skin temperature, stress, activity levels and sleep. There's also menstrual tracking and a Baby Prep mode to support ovulation prediction.
Alongside these core features, RingConn offers a few more advanced tools that are designed to help it stand out from rivals. One of the most useful is sleep apnea monitoring. Once enabled, it monitors for the core signs of sleep apnea and provides short-term risk indicators alongside longer-term trends.
Like any wearable health feature, it's not designed to diagnose a medical condition. But I think it could be useful if you're concerned about your sleep quality or breathing patterns and want some additional information before you speak to a doctor.
New for the Gen 3 is a built-in haptic motor, which means the ring can now vibrate for health alerts, inactivity reminders and low-battery warnings.
At first, I was conflicted about this addition. Part of the appeal of smart rings for me is that they collect data in the background without demanding attention in the way a smartwatch can. Fortunately, RingConn has taken a restrained approach. The vibrations are subtle, focused on health-related notifications rather than phone alerts and can be disabled entirely if you'd prefer that.
Another notable addition is RingConn's vascular health tracking. Rather than attempting to estimate blood pressure directly, the feature combines overnight vascular load data with blood pressure readings and lifestyle information to provide longer-term cardiovascular insights.
To use it, you'll need to periodically enter blood pressure readings from a traditional blood pressure cuff. Initially, I wasn't convinced of the value of this feature. Wouldn’t you just use a cuff instead of the ring if you have one? But it became clear during testing that the goal here isn't to replace a blood pressure monitor. Instead, it's designed to help identify broader patterns over time.
One reason for the confusion is likely that in the app this section is labelled as 'blood pressure trends', which RingConn tells me is out-of-date copy and will be changed to 'vascular insights' soon to make it clear this isn't just a blood pressure reading feature.
Because the data you get here is about circulation stress tracking, which RingConn describes as a measure of how effectively your body moves between activity and recovery. Results are then also broken down into areas such as day-night rhythm, sleep breathing, post-exercise recovery and stress response.
The insights aren't especially deep, and if anything is flagged you'll need to go and search for what it means, but they're among the most detailed explanations available in the RingConn app and provide useful context without becoming overwhelming.
- Features Score: 4/5
RingConn Gen 3: Performance
- Clean, easy-to-use app
- Excellent battery life
- Strong sleep and wellness tracking
As with any smart ring, the Gen 3 relies heavily on its app, and RingConn gets a lot right here. While it doesn't feel quite as polished as Oura's software, I found it easy to navigate through the different menus. I also liked the flower-like Wellness Balance graphic at the top of the dashboard, which provides a quick visual snapshot of your overall health.
The app makes it easy to check key metrics at a glance, while more detailed charts, historical trends and explanations are there if you click through into each dedicated section, including sleep, activity and stress. Stress tracking was a particular highlight, making it easy to spot recurring patterns and periods of higher pressure throughout the day.
Some of the written insights can feel a little generic though, as daily summaries occasionally surfaced observations that felt obvious or lacked enough context to be genuinely useful. Sleep insights tended to be more helpful, with more detailed explanations and recommendations.
Sleep tracking is one of RingConn's strongest areas. The app presents sleep duration, efficiency, stages, overnight heart rate and movement data clearly without overwhelming you with information. During testing, it also handled my occasionally unusual sleep schedule surprisingly well, which meant that on nights when I woke up for an hour in the early morning before falling back asleep, RingConn correctly identified this as a brief 'awake' period rather than ending the sleep session entirely.
In terms of accuracy, I wore the RingConn Gen 3 alongside a Whoop 5.0. The two devices produced very similar results. Whoop measured a 84% sleep performance, 6 hours and 31 minutes of sleep and a 49bpm average overnight heart rate. RingConn gave me a 77 sleep score, recorded 6 hours and16 minutes of sleep with a 48bpm average overnight heart rate
Sleep stage breakdowns also aligned closely, with only minor differences in deep and REM sleep estimates. No wearable tracks sleep perfectly, but the results were broadly consistent.
I also appreciated how RingConn handles unusual readings. Rather than generating alarming warnings whenever a metric moves outside of its normal range, the app generally presents changes with reasonable context. I'd still like more explanation in some areas, particularly when a metric is flagged. I was often felt feeling a little frustrated at the lack of context and additional information as to why a reading deviated and what that really means. But the overall approach feels useful and sensible.
Sleep apnea monitoring is well implemented here. The feature presents trends clearly, includes some useful explanations and feels more mature than some of the app's other health insights. It's worth noting though that monitoring won't function properly once battery levels drop below 30%.
Exercise tracking is more basic than what you'll get from a dedicated sports watch, although that's true of most smart rings. During testing, the ring automatically detected walking, running and strength-training sessions without requiring manual input. You just need to acknowledge it’s identified your activity correctly and there are a wide range to choose from.
In the activity section you’ll find useful information like activity intensity, active time, calories burned and step count, which should be enough for most users.
Step tracking was accurate, although RingConn did seem to slightly under report compared to other devices. On one test day it recorded 5,167 steps versus 5,500 on the Whoop, a pattern I noticed in a few other comparisons.
Battery life is still one of RingConn's biggest strengths. The company claims between 11 and 14 days per charge, and in my testing the ring lasted nearly 12.5 days with both vascular insights and haptic alerts enabled.
That comfortably exceeds most rivals these days. For comparison, the Oura Ring 5 offers up to 7 days, the Samsung Galaxy Ring up to 7 days, while the Ultrahuman Ring Air and Circular Ring 2 both offer around 6 days.
For me, this is one of the RingConn's biggest selling points. The less often you need to remove a wearable for charging, the more likely you are to wear it consistently and collect uninterrupted data. RingConn also displays both remaining battery percentage and an estimate of days remaining in the map, which is a small but useful touch.
Overall, the RingConn Gen 3 delivers a strong experience. The app isn't quite as refined as Oura's, and some insights could go further, but the combination of comprehensive health tracking, clear data presentation, excellent battery life and a subscription-free model makes it one of the most compelling smart rings currently available.
- Performance score: 4/5
RingConn Gen 3: Scorecard
| Category | Comment | Score | 
| Value | There's no subscription and it undercuts major rivals. But not by all that much. | 3.5/5 | 
| Design | It's lightweight, comfortable and has a non-standard squared circle design. Nice glossy finish with several more available in this version too. There's no wearing indicator and sizing might differ this time around. | 4.5/5 | 
| Features | A solid set of health and wellbeing features. Vascular insights are welcome, though not intuitive to use — you'll need a separate cuff. Otherwise, it is pretty similar to the Gen 2 that came before it. | 4/5 | 
| Performance | Solid insights presented simply in the app. Which is a little less refined than rivals, but easy to use. The battery life is standout and I found myself really engaging with the data rather than forgetting to check — a testament to a solid experience. | 4/5 | 
RingConn Gen 3: Should I buy?
Buy it if...
You don't want to pay a subscription
All of the features on offer here are free, which sets it apart from rivals like Oura that charge a monthly fee.
You want a light and comfortable smart ring
It's very easy to wear, even at night. And despite reported changes to sizing, I got the size I usually wear with no issues.
You want general health insights
Look, smart rings are not the last word in fitness tracking. There's some of it here but they're best at general health insights and an overall picture of your wellbeing.
Don't buy it if...
You have the Gen 2 or Air
Yes, there are some significant improvements here, but not everyone would be able to justify an upgrade. It depends whether the changes are a priority for you.
You want to save money
Compared to rivals, it's solid value. But there are now cheaper options that might not beat the RingConn Gen 3, but do the basics well.
You're considering Oura
As you'll learn below, Oura is pricier with a monthly subscription. But it is an elevated experience over RingConn in most ways.
Also consider
Oura Ring 5
The Oura Ring 5 is here and it's one of the best choices out there, especially now the latest version is even slimmer than previous iterations. We rated its improved design and comfort in our recent review. Yes, it's more expensive than the RingConn Gen 3 and you'll need to add on the recurring monthly subscription. But if it's the most advanced smart ring you're after and you're willing to pay for it, take a look at the Oura Ring 5 instead.
Read our full Oura Ring 5 review
RingConn Gen 2
I know, I know. This is the older model, but it's been significantly reduced now the Gen 3 is here. Which makes it even better value. Granted, you're not getting the improved battery life, extra finish options, upgraded tracking and vascular insights. But if saving money is a priority, you find a good bargain and you don't need the latest tech, it's a solid choice in my books.
Read our full RingConn Gen 2 review
How I tested
I tested the Ringconn Gen 3 for just over 2 weeks. I wore it all day and all night, only taking it off to either charge it or lift weights — I've learned many times in the past that smart rings are very easy to scratch with metal dumbbells. The smart ring was on throughout workouts, while I was working, out socializing, relaxing on an evening and sleeping at night.
I've been reviewing smart rings since the very first version of the Oura ring came out back in 2017. Since then, I've tested almost every generation from every smart ring brand that came after it. This puts me in a solid position to not only test the newest rings, but compare the models, tell you which one might be right for you and bring you loads of context about the smart ring space.
- First reviewed: June 2026
Becca is a contributor to TechRadar, a freelance journalist and author. She’s been writing about consumer tech and popular science for more than ten years, covering all kinds of topics, including why robots have eyes and whether we’ll experience the overview effect one day. She’s particularly interested in VR/AR, wearables, digital health, space tech and chatting to experts and academics about the future. She’s contributed to TechRadar, T3, Wired, New Scientist, The Guardian, Inverse and many more. Her first book, Screen Time, came out in January 2021 with Bonnier Books. She loves science-fiction, brutalist architecture, and spending too much time floating through space in virtual reality.
